title: A Friar, a Philosopher, and 90,000 Notes: So How Do You Actually Read a Book Right?
author: William Meller
summary: William Meller traces a chain of three books on reading and note-taking: Antonin Sertillanges's The Intellectual Life (1921), Mortimer Adler's How to Read a Book (1940) and Sonke Ahrens's How to Take Smart Notes (2017). He argues that despite the explosion of digital second-brain tooling, the three authors reached the same conclusion, that reading which does not trigger an internal dialogue will not stay in memory. Sertillanges recommended index cards and deep focus on few books, Adler framed reading as an active debate with the author conducted in the margins, and Ahrens, through Luhmann's 90,000 cards, insists an idea earns a card only when expressed in your own words. Meller's own practice is to keep an insight only if he can explain it without looking at the source. He concludes that modern apps rename old tools while the mental demand stays the same.
points: Sertillanges, Adler and Ahrens, writing across nearly a century, independently concluded that reading without an internal response is just turning pages.
Adler's stages of reading (elementary, inspectional, analytical, syntopical) treat reading as an active debate with the author, including questions written in the margins.
Ahrens's core rule is that an idea does not earn a card until you can express it entirely in your own words.
Meller keeps an insight in his permanent notes only if he can explain it clearly without looking at the source, and he does the archiving himself rather than trusting software.
Productivity software gives new names to old tools, but the demand never changes: you must put an idea to work or it never becomes yours.
quotes: Leaving an idea to a half-awake brain, he explained, is like writing words on water. By sunrise, nothing remains.
He reminds us, with a quiet honesty that might feel almost jarring today, that we read to sharpen our thinking, not to collect vanity metrics.

Adler broke reading down into clear stages (elementary, inspectional, analytical, and syntopical), and he defended an approach that must have felt radical at the time: real reading is an active debate with the author.
His core principle remains the most demanding of the three: an idea does not earn a card until you can express it entirely in your own words.
These three thinkers arrived at identical conclusions from separate worlds: reading that fails to trigger an internal dialogue will never stay in your memory.
An insight only enters my permanent notes if I can explain it clearly without looking at the source.
Modern apps give new names to old tools, yet the mental demand never changes: you must put an idea to work, or it never becomes yours.
